[] Absolutely — our relationship with routines can change quite a bit over time, and there are a lot of subtle factors behind it. In the evenings, your body’s natural circadian rhythm is winding down and, as we get older, that rhythm can shift a little earlier in the day. That means the same after‑work activity that once felt energizing might now feel like it takes more effort or mental preparation.

There are also environmental factors at play — changes in daylight across the seasons, differences in temperature or humidity, even local noise or traffic patterns can subtly affect how appealing something feels. If you’ve had a particularly stimulating or stressful day, your brain may lean toward lower‑energy restorative activities rather than something that requires you to get back out and about.

On the psychological side, there’s the ‘novelty effect’: a routine you once loved may not provide the same spark if your lifestyle, priorities, or tastes have shifted. It’s similar to a ballplayer who’s always batted cleanup suddenly finding that a different spot in the batting order suits where they are in their career — the player’s core skills haven’t vanished, but the context has changed, and so has the optimal role.

It’s also worth noting that small changes in personal interests can play a big role too. Even if you’re still active and community‑oriented, you might find new ways to unwind after work that feel more satisfying in your current season of life — maybe catching a game on TV, meeting friends for dinner, or diving into a good sports documentary. It’s all part of the natural ebb and flow of habits, and adjusting them doesn’t mean you’ve ‘lost’ anything — you’ve just re‑balanced your lineup to fit today’s game conditions.
